🟢 what does Fascia look like?  Video credit to @bradley_blair_osteopath Fascia is a generic term that describes any sheath, sheet, or other dissectible mass of tissue that attaches, wraps, and/or separates the deep structures of the body.  In general, there are two types of fascia: Superficial fascia Deep fascia The superficial fascia (i.e. tela subcutanea, hypodermis, subcutaneous tissue) is used to describe the connective that separates the skin from the underlying muscle tissue.  The deep fascia is a dense, organised, connective tissue located deep to the skin and subcutaneous tissue. It surrounds muscles, viscera and related structures.  Depending on its location, there are several types of deep fascia. These include:  Fasciae of muscles (i.e. fasciae musculorum) Fasciae of body cavities (i.e. fasciae cavitatum trunci) The main function of the fasciae is to protect and support deep structures and organs of the body. In addition, fasciae reduce friction between muscles, transmit movement from muscle to bones and sometimes serve as the attachment point for skeletal muscles. As I’ve moved through my 20s, I’ve realised that mobility training isn’t optional - it’s a necessity for keeping my body strong, pain-free, and moving with ease. Here’s how I keep mobility work a consistent part of my busy week: ➡️ Dynamic warm-ups: I start each workout with dynamic drills instead of static stretches to wake up my joints and prep for more intense movement.  ➡️ Post-workout mobility: I like to end with targeted mobility work, like thoracic spine rotations or deep hip stretches, to keep my body moving well and prevent stiffness.  ➡️ Animal Flow: This form of quadrupedal movement training (QMT) is all about improving range of motion and joint strength in a way that’s both functional and fun! Even just 20 minutes of Animal Flow is enough stimulus to better the health of your body. ➡️ Mobility in strength training: Some of my favourite mobility exercises are also great in resistance workouts, like front-foot elevated lunges and dumbbell Y raises. These moves improve shoulder and hip mobility, which means better posture and more balanced strength. As we get into our 30s, prioritising mobility is key to maintaining an active lifestyle and keeping aches and pains at bay. So if you haven’t already, it’s time to make mobility a regular part of your training! I know that total body pain is experienced by many women in the south asian community, I will even go as far as saying from speaking to and working with women it is their most dominant menopause symptom. Life debilitating to many.  But it’s commonly not associated with menopause and they are often dismissed and disregarded. Terms such as Mrs Bibi/Mrs Begum syndrome are used about such women - more on this in future posts. If they are fortunate enough to be taken seriously by their doctor, this pain can often be contributed to depression, fibromyalgia and other health conditions and their declining hormones are not considered.  There is so much we can do ourselves to help reduce and manage this total body pain as well as looking at HRT if we are still struggling after addressing our life management. Can you see what I’m doing? 🤔🔎 Blink and you’ll miss it!  You might not be able to tell, but I’m pushing my hip to its absolute limit, fighting for more space in my hip joint. Creating this space strengthens the tissue surrounding the hip joint and supports more freedom to move.  Our hips have a big impact on our bodies and can dictate our ability to move. Restriction can unknowingly be the lead cause of aches and pains elsewhere around our body, so it’s incredibly important that we look after our hip health! So, what am I doing in the video? This movement sequence is called ‘PAILS & RAILS’ (Progressive Angular Isometric Loading & Regressive Angular Isometric Loading) The aim; to gradually apply load in the hip joint over a 15-30 second period at your active end range in external rotation followed by 90-100% max effort internal rotation without any compensation from another part of your body. What is your active end range? Your active end range is the furthest point you can physically move your joint to without the use of additional force. What is a compensation?  A compensation is a movement from another part of your body which essentially helps you get into the position you need/want (cheating) PAILS & RAILS are an excellent movement system to help strengthen your joints and improve your mobility.  This isn’t a simple system to use and finding the right placement to get the maximum impact won’t happen immediately. Hormone replacement therapy is given to relieve the symptoms of perimenopause and menopause.  Oestrogen is given to help relieve the symptoms , usually as a patch, gel, spray or oral tablet.  If you have a uterus  (womb) and you take oestrogen it can cause the lining of the womb to thicken, so progesterone is given to protect the womb from the thickening effects of oestrogen and to protect from endometrial cancer (cancer of the lining of the womb). It is really important to remember to take this exactly as it has been prescribed to you by your doctor. It is important not to adjust the dose of your HRT yourself. Some women without a womb also are advised to take progesterone.  This information is for guidance only and should not be used for individual medical advice , please discuss with your own doctor if you have any questions about your hormone replacement therapy. When you have musculoskeletal pain and dysfunction, it stands to reason you want it resolved as soon as possible right? "You fixed someone else in just one treatment, why not me? You might ask. Well the fact of the matter is that in chronic cases the pathology is far more established and will take longer to gain normal function again. When I'm assessing you and I don't see a big difference in your functional short leg, then that means there are probably multiple layers at play. The layers have piled on top of each other to make it appear like there's not a big leg length discrepancy. When I take one layer away, eg by treating your neck, (which I'll always do, even though your presenting symptom was back pain, sciatica, knee pain etc) then the short leg can become even shorter or change to the opposite leg signifying deeper layers of soft tissue dysfunction. You'll recognise this as me dorsiflexing your feet and flexing your knees at various points during the treatment. I'm looking for resolution of these layers by achieving symmetry, or to see if your body is ready to reveal the next layer while you are on the table. Maybe it will hang onto it, and slowly allow it to come to the surface while you are rehabilitating in between sessions. This is the importance of your follow up sessions. If you only attend the one treatment, there's no understanding on either of our parts about what state of equilibrium you have reached since I put the intervention in. Your body will display it's issues in the order it wants. Sometimes you will feel amazing and pain free after your treatment, and sometimes your symptoms may get worse or new ones may arise before things can settle down longer term. There is no right and wrong about it, it's unique to the individual. I firmly believe that you should also be accountable for your recovery, so I will always provide detailed aftercare advice that compliments and facilitates your healing. It's above and beyond what you need to know as part of your session, but I do this because I care about your well-being. I know what chronic pain feels like, and I am ever so grateful to the amazing therapists & teachers that have treated me over the last few years, restoring me to a pain free and fully functioning, happy and healthy life and to Tom Bowen for making it possible with his exceptional work. 🙏🙌 What makes a chronic case? You DON’T have to RUN 🏃‍♀️ or JUMP 🦘 to be fit reasonably! If I hadn’t had so many injuries, suffered from arthritis, spent time being less mobile, or felt as stiff as the proverbial stump on a cold, damp day, I would it hard to empathise with the majority of the clients I have helped improve their fitness. Because fitness has been an integral part of my lifestyle for almost five decades, and because of my passion for feeling fit, strong, and healthy, I have managed to find every conceivable way to overcome these limitations.  Pain 😣 or getting out of pain is a hell a motivator 💪, and I love helping others to reduce theirs. I’m sure that I speak for most fitness coaches when I say this: when people are unwilling to discuss their fitness with me when they enquire into my services, it is soooo frustrating!! This is not a stain on their character, by the way, but when they want a price for my help without giving telling me their goals, their fitness history, their nutritional habits, their likes and dislikes, and most importantly their physical condition, how can I give them a price? Fitness is not a one-size-fits-all service. As a fitness professional, I take client safety 🧷 seriously. To keep a client safe, especial the over 50s, I must take their medical conditions and injuries into account, so that when I write their workouts, they have exercise options that suit them (not everyone else), ones that will not exacerbate an existing injury, or cause a new one. It’s a question of risk assessment and risk management and making sure that a client exercises in a way that helps them improve their physical condition, not hinder it. Now here’s the good news, unless you’re striving to be an elite sportsperson you can still achieve a good level of fitness without having to run or jump and causing impact to sensitive areas of the body. You DON’T have to RUN 🏃‍♀️ or JUMP 🦘 to be fit reasonably! If I hadn’t had so many injuries, suffered from arthritis, spent time being less mobile, or felt as stiff as the proverbial stump on a cold, damp day, I would it hard to empathise with the majority of the clients I have helped improve their fitness. Because fitness has been an integral part of my lifestyle for almost five decades, and because of my passion for feeling fit, strong, and healthy, I have managed to find every conceivable way to overcome these limitations.  Pain 😣 or getting out of pain is a hell a motivator 💪, and I love helping others to reduce theirs. I’m sure that I speak for most fitness coaches when I say this: when people are unwilling to discuss their fitness with me when they enquire into my services, it is soooo frustrating!! This is not a stain on their character, by the way, but when they want a price for my help without giving telling me their goals, their fitness history, their nutritional habits, their likes and dislikes, and most importantly their physical condition, how can I give them a price? Fitness is not a one-size-fits-all service. As a fitness professional, I take client safety 🧷 seriously. To keep a client safe, especial the over 50s, I must take their medical conditions and injuries into account, so that when I write their workouts, they have exercise options that suit them (not everyone else), ones that will not exacerbate an existing injury, or cause a new one. It’s a question of risk assessment and risk management and making sure that a client exercises in a way that helps them improve their physical condition, not hinder it. Now here’s the good news, unless you’re striving to be an elite sportsperson you can still achieve a good level of fitness without having to run or jump and causing impact to sensitive areas of the body.
